items.description: The contribution of demand deposits, usually call and check accounts decreased to 7.8% in August 2026 from 10.6% in August 2025. Similarly, the contribution of savings and time deposits declined to 7.0% from 7.3% over the same comparative period. However, the contribution of foreign currency deposits (FCDs) to money supply growth increased significantly to 1.6% in August 2026, compared with negative 4.0% in August 2025. According to the Bank of Ghana, this mainly reflected the effect of the discontinued dual currency Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) policy. Similarly, the contribution of currency outside banks increased to 4.0% in August 2026 from 2.7% in August 2025, reflecting increased demand for cash holdings. Meanwhile, the annual growth in broad money supply (M2+) increased to 20.4% in August 2026, from 16.6% in August 2025. The Bank of Ghana attributed the increase in broad money growth to a significant build-up in Net Domestic Assets (NDA), while growth in Net Foreign Assets (NFA) declined to moderate the growth in M2+. The contribution of NFA to total liquidity growth decreased marginally to 7.2% in August 2026 from 8.8% in August 2025. This reflects in the moderation in the rate of foreign asset accumulation in the banking sector during the period under review.

items.title: Chinese FM holds talks with Azerbaijani counterpart
items.description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Thursday. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that in recent years, China-Azerbaijan relations have entered the fast track, achieved leapfrog development and reached their best period in history, opening up broad prospects for the future. The sound development of bilateral relations has benefited from the high level of mutual trust between leaders of the two countries and the strategic guarantee they provide, enabling the two sides to firmly support each other on issues concerning their respective core interests, continuously consolidate the political foundation of bilateral relations and create important conditions for strengthening cooperation, Wang said. As a long-term strategic partner, China will continue to support Azerbaijan in accelerating its development and revitalization, he added. China appreciates Azerbaijan's work during its chairmanship of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) and supports Azerbaijan in playing a greater role within the CICA and in international affairs, Wang said. Noting that next year will mark the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Azerbaijan, Wang said that China stands ready to work with Azerbaijan to implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, and take the anniversary as an opportunity to jointly accelerate their respective modernization drives and benefit the two peoples. For his part, Bayramov said Azerbaijan and China are sincere friends and reliable partners, with a long-standing friendship, increasingly close exchanges at all levels and bilateral relations reaching an unprecedented level. Azerbaijan firmly adheres to the one-China principle and stands ready to work with China, under the guidance of the two heads of state, to advance their comprehensive strategic partnership, strengthen cooperation in areas such as energy, transport, climate change, artificial intelligence, and people-to-people and cultural exchanges, and step up efforts in the Belt and Road cooperation and support to the Middle Corridor, Bayramov said. The two sides also had an in-depth exchange of views on advancing bilateral practical cooperation in the next phase and on international and regional issues of common concern.

items.title: Couverture sanitaire : des fragilités financières menacent la pérennité de certains régimes
items.description: L’élargissement de la couverture sanitaire à près de 80 % de la population ne suffit pas à garantir la pérennité du système, prévient Abderrahim Chaffai, président de l’Autorité de contrôle des assurances et de la prévoyance sociale. Il appelle à évaluer séparément les régimes d’assurance-maladie obligatoire et à adapter leur financement aux besoins des bénéficiaires. La généralisation de la couverture sanitaire au Maroc ne pourra tenir ses promesses sans une consolidation de l’équilibre financier des régimes d’assurance-maladie obligatoire (AMO). C’est l’avertissement formulé par Abderrahim Chaffai, président de l’Autorité de contrôle des assurances et de la prévoyance sociale (ACAPS), lors d’un colloque international organisé mercredi 14 octobre à Marrakech par le Conseil de la concurrence, autour du thème « La politique de santé au Maroc : concurrence, régulation et gouvernance à l’ère de la couverture sanitaire universelle ». Si l’extension de la couverture sanitaire a permis de faire passer le taux de population couverte d’environ 40 % à 80 %, cette progression ne saurait, à elle seule, constituer un indicateur de réussite, a souligné le responsable. Encore faut-il que les régimes disposent des ressources nécessaires pour honorer leurs engagements et garantir la continuité de la prise en charge sur le long terme. L’évaluation du dispositif doit ainsi dépasser le simple décompte des bénéficiaires et des cotisations collectées pour mesurer la capacité réelle de chaque régime à assurer sa pérennité. Cette équation financière se révèle particulièrement complexe pour les travailleurs non salariés et les actifs du secteur informel, dont les contributions sont plus difficiles à mobiliser de manière régulière. Pour l’ACAPS, l’enjeu consiste à élargir la base des cotisants tout en tenant compte des disparités de revenus et des capacités contributives de chaque catégorie. Une approche uniforme risquerait, selon Chaffai, de négliger les différences de situation économique et de consommation de soins entre les assurés. Des situations financières contrastées selon les régimes La solidité du système suppose, en premier lieu, de ne pas considérer l’assurance-maladie obligatoire comme un ensemble financièrement homogène. Les régimes présentent des différences de structure, de financement et de profils de bénéficiaires qui justifient, selon le président de l’ACAPS, une évaluation distincte de leur situation. À cet égard, le régime des salariés présenterait un équilibre financier, selon son appréciation. D’autres composantes connaissent en revanche des difficultés, notamment la Caisse nationale des organismes de prévoyance sociale (CNOPS), dont la situation soulève des questions relatives aux équilibres financiers et aux réserves. Une lecture globale des comptes risque ainsi de masquer les fragilités propres à certains dispositifs. Pour les identifier, l’ACAPS procède chaque année à un diagnostic de chaque régime et partage ses conclusions avec les caisses concernées. Ces échanges doivent permettre d’analyser les insuffisances constatées et de définir les mesures correctives appropriées. Les observations concernant le secteur public sont transmises aux autorités gouvernementales compétentes. L’objectif est de passer d’une appréciation générale de la couverture sanitaire à une analyse plus fine des risques financiers, afin d’intervenir sur les mécanismes qui fragilisent chaque régime. Le secteur informel au cœur de l’équation L’intégration des travailleurs non salariés et des actifs du secteur informel constitue un autre défi majeur. La régularité des cotisations et leur adéquation avec les dépenses de santé représentent deux variables déterminantes pour la viabilité du dispositif. Abderrahim Chaffai a notamment fait état d’une proportion d’environ 45 % de personnes malades parmi les bénéficiaires de l’une des catégories évoquées lors de son intervention, selon les chiffres figurant dans la transcription de ses propos. Cette donnée illustre les tensions susceptibles d’apparaître lorsque les besoins en soins sont importants au regard des cotisations effectivement perçues. Dans ce contexte, la couverture sanitaire solidaire nécessite, selon lui, des mécanismes de financement adaptés, une meilleure maîtrise des dépenses et un élargissement de la base contributive. Ces ajustements doivent toutefois tenir compte des écarts de capacité économique entre les travailleurs du secteur formel et ceux du secteur informel. L’enjeu est de préserver le principe de solidarité sans compromettre l’équilibre des régimes. L’augmentation du nombre de bénéficiaires ne doit ni aggraver les déséquilibres financiers ni réduire la capacité des organismes gestionnaires à respecter leurs engagements. Anticiper les risques plutôt que subir les déséquilibres Au-delà du suivi des comptes, le président de l’ACAPS plaide pour une approche prospective de la soutenabilité financière de la couverture sanitaire. Les évolutions démographiques, les variations des cotisations et la progression des dépenses de santé doivent être intégrées aux évaluations, plutôt que de s’en tenir aux résultats financiers d’un exercice donné. Les données relatives aux cotisations, aux prestations servies et aux réserves doivent faire l’objet d’un suivi régulier, complété par des études prospectives dont les conclusions seraient partagées avec l’ensemble des acteurs concernés. Une telle démarche permettrait d’anticiper les risques et de prendre des mesures correctives avant que les difficultés ne s’aggravent. Cette exigence de rigueur financière ne doit toutefois pas se faire au détriment des droits des assurés. Abderrahim Chaffai a rappelé la nécessité de leur garantir un accès effectif aux services de santé, sans exclusion, tout en conciliant les impératifs de protection sociale avec les ressources disponibles. La pérennité de la couverture sanitaire universelle dépendra, en définitive, de la capacité des organismes de contrôle, des caisses gestionnaires et des départements gouvernementaux à coordonner leurs interventions. Pour l’ACAPS, il s’agit de corriger les déséquilibres propres à chaque régime afin de préserver les droits des bénéficiaires et d’assurer la continuité du système sur le long terme. The post Couverture sanitaire : des fragilités financières menacent la pérennité de certains régimes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Chinese FM puts forward four proposals on boosting CICA cooperation
items.description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi put forward four proposals on boosting cooperation among member states of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) on Thursday while attending the Seventh Summit of the CICA. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that the CICA is a platform for dialogue and cooperation initiated and jointly built by Asian countries. Since its establishment, the CICA has actively championed the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, systematically advanced cooperation on confidence building measures, consistently practiced multilateralism, and worked tirelessly to strengthen the foundation of trust for peace and security in Asia. China highly appreciates Azerbaijan's efforts during its CICA chairmanship to advance CICA cooperation, and stands ready to continue its strong support for and active participation in the CICA process, Wang said. Amid accelerating changes unseen in a century, only by fostering a sense of community with a shared future, standing on the right side of history, and upholding solidarity and cooperation can Asian countries stand at the forefront of the times, turn crises into opportunities and jointly create a better future, he said. Wang put forward four proposals: First, jointly safeguard peace and stability. Asia does not need a Cold War mentality and does not welcome bloc confrontation. Asia's problems should ultimately be addressed by the people of Asia through solidarity and cooperation, and Asia's security should be ensured by upholding the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. Second, jointly promote prosperity and revitalization. Development is the master key to solving all problems. Efforts should be made to better align high-quality Belt and Road cooperation with the development initiatives of various countries, safeguard an open environment for cooperation, advance trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, ensure the stable and efficient operation of international transport corridors, and strengthen supply security for critical raw materials, energy resources and food, so that Asian countries can work together to accelerate their progress toward modernization. Third, jointly promote exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. Asia is the continent with the greatest diversity of civilizations. Efforts should be made to firmly promote the Asian values of peace, cooperation, openness and inclusiveness, respect countries' independent choices of development paths and governance models, deepen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism and health, as well as among women's and youth groups, media organizations and think tanks, and promote people-to-people exchanges and closer bonds between peoples, so that diverse civilizations can learn from one another and flourish together. Fourth, jointly improve global governance. Efforts should be made to reinvigorate the authority and role of the United Nations, uphold the basic norms governing international relations established by the UN Charter, strengthen capacities in digital governance, disaster prevention and mitigation, and public health, and jointly build a more efficient, inclusive and resilient governance system in Asia. Wang stressed that China will remain firmly committed to the path of peaceful development, bring greater stability to the international landscape through its own high-quality development, and provide stronger impetus for global growth. China stands ready to work with all parties to build consensus, deepen cooperation and jointly build a peaceful, stable, prosperous, open and inclusive Asian community with a shared future, making greater Asian contribution to world peace and development, Wang said. Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev briefed attendees on the work undertaken by Azerbaijan during its two-year CICA chairmanship and put forward proposals for cooperation. Participants exchanged views on the security and development situation in the CICA region and the implementation of confidence building measures. They agreed that CICA member states should practice multilateralism, strengthen solidarity and cooperation, address common challenges, safeguard the common interests of the Global South, and promote peace and development in Asia. The summit adopted and issued the Baku Declaration of the Seventh CICA Summit. On the sidelines of the summit, Wang also met separately with Israeli President Isaac Herzog, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Palestinian Foreign Minister Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, and had friendly exchanges with dignitaries from various countries. (With input from Xinhua)

items.title: Fiscal policy implementation poses downside risk to inflation – BoG
items.description: The Bank of Ghana has described the implementation of the government’s fiscal policy in 2026 as posing a downside risk to inflation. According to its Monetary Policy Report, the US-Iran conflict, with its impact on crude oil prices, may put pressure on the government to offer periodic reliefs, which may pose some challenges to the budget. “The rest of 2026 is expected to witness a scale-up in government spending and there are concerns over the absorptive capacity of contractors executing government projects, which could have implications for inflation”. It, however, assured that the government remains committed to controlling expenditure, boosting efficiency gains, and adhering to value-for-money standards. At the same time, it pointed out that the government aims to strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation to enable it to meet debt service obligations, thus ensuring long-term debt sustainability. “It must also be noted that the full completion of bilateral and commercial debt restructuring is expected to lead to an increase in future debt service payments”. With respect to debt sustainability, it called for the strengthening of fiscal management to reduce the rate of debt accumulation and the resulting debt servicing costs. “The currently high proportion of short-term debt heightens rollover and refinancing risks, potentially limiting the fiscal space for productive investments and growth-enhancing expenditures. In the long term, higher domestic savings will be required to meet external debt repayments, with potential implications for exchange rate stability”, it added. The Central Bank concluded that sustained real Gross Domestic Product growth, lower real interest rates, and continued exchange rate stability are the prerequisites for improving Ghana’s debt sustainability and preserving its status of moderate risk of debt distress.

items.title: Organised Labour should seek fair adjustment, not excessive pay rise – Labour consultant
items.description: Labour consultant Austin Gamey has urged Organised Labour to pursue a fair adjustment in the 2027 base pay negotiations, cautioning that excessively high expectations could delay an agreement with government. He said the proposed increase should be guided by economic data, including previous inflation projections, actual inflation figures and current forecasts, rather than perceptions about the cost of living. Speaking in an interview on Joy FM’s Newsnight o thursday, octoer 15, Mr Gamey said labour was justified in seeking an adjustment but needed to ensure its expectations reflected prevailing economic conditions. “I wouldn’t like to use the word demand, for an adjustment that is commensurate with the situation on our hands. But it has to be based upon data,” he said. Mr Gamey explained that Organised Labour should first establish the extent to which workers’ purchasing power needed to be restored before determining any additional adjustment to cushion them against rising living costs. He added that workers’ productivity and the country’s economic performance should also inform the negotiations. According to him, pushing for an excessively high increase could create further inflationary pressures and undermine the intended benefits of higher wages. “The macro indicators are quite reasonable, and therefore you can’t go too high, otherwise you’re rather creating further inflation in the system, and it’s your own making,” he said. Mr Gamey’s comments come as government and Organised Labour prepare to negotiate the 2027 base pay, with the current agreement reflecting a nine per cent increase across the Single Spine Salary Structure for 2026. Organised Labour has maintained that slowing inflation has not translated into lower market prices or restored workers’ purchasing power, and intends to make a strong case for a higher adjustment. However, Mr Gamey questioned what he described as an overemphasis on the high cost of living, arguing that prices of some commodities, including tomatoes and ginger, had begun to decline. He urged stakeholders to rely on economic data in assessing price movements rather than generalising about the cost of living. On the possibility of a deadlock before the 2027 Budget is presented, Mr Gamey said the parties should resort to established dispute-resolution mechanisms rather than allow negotiations to stall. He suggested mediation through the National Labour Commission or an alternative dispute resolution centre to help government and organised labour reach an agreement.

items.title: Sanwo-Olu orders immediate repairs of Lagos roads
items.description: By Olasunkanmi Akoni Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, has directed the State Public Works Corporation (LSPWC) to commence immediate road reconstruction and rehabilitation across the state, taking advantage of the dry season to address deteriorating infrastructure. The General Manager of LSPWC, Engr. Tokunbo Ajanaku, disclosed this on Thursday during an inspection tour of ongoing projects, assuring residents of improved road networks as weather conditions become more favourable for construction work. Ajanaku said Oshodi-Isolo Local Government Area was a major focus of the exercise, with reconstruction underway on Godwin Omonuwa Road, Taiwo Street, Salamotu Street, Peter Agah Street and Ibeh Street. He said the projects were undertaken at the governor’s direction to address infrastructure deficits and improve connectivity within communities. “These roads are important links within the Oshodi-Isolo axis, serving residents, traders, business owners and other road users daily. “Their reconstruction will not only improve mobility but also reduce transportation costs, enhance road safety, boost commercial activities and create a more conducive environment for businesses and residents,” Ajanaku said. He added that the inspection covered other ongoing rehabilitation projects across the state, including Ogunnusi Road in Ojodu Local Council Development Area (LCDA), Awolowo Way in Ikeja Local Government Area, Lanre Awolokun Road and Idowu Olaitan Street in Shomolu, as well as Idimu-Ikotun Road in Alimosho. According to him, heavy rainfall often limits asphalt laying, but the corporation maintained emergency palliative interventions during the rainy season to keep critical roads motorable. He said the agency was now shifting towards more comprehensive and durable repairs with the return of dry weather. Ajanaku added that much of the maintenance and asphalt-laying work was being carried out at night, under appropriate safety measures, to minimise traffic congestion across the metropolis. He appealed to residents to be patient, explaining that road repairs were prioritised based on road conditions, traffic volume and the urgency of intervention. The general manager said the corporation would progressively extend its operations to other parts of the state. He also urged residents to protect public infrastructure by avoiding practices that contribute to road deterioration, including dumping refuse in drainage channels, spilling petroleum products and discharging wastewater onto roads. “Our roads are our collective heritage. Government has the responsibility to provide and maintain them, but citizens also have a duty to protect them. Road preservation must therefore be a shared responsibility,” Ajanaku said. BoG maintains medium-term inflation target of 8 ± 2%
items.description: The Bank of Ghana has maintained its medium-term inflation target of 8 ± 2% barring any shocks. This follows a third consecutive increase in year-on-year inflation in September 2026. At the 132nd Monetary Policy Committee, the Committee expressed concerns about the elevated external risks arising from the global economy amid relatively favourable domestic conditions. The Committee also observed an uptick in headline inflation in August, driven largely by an increase in non-food inflation. Despite this uptick, the Committee noted easing inflation expectations and core inflation over the period, suggesting moderating underlying inflationary pressures. Following its evaluation of global and domestic developments, it maintained that headline inflation remained on course to return to its target range of 8±2% over the medium term, barring any shocks. “Upward adjustments in utility tariffs, rising ex-pump petroleum prices, strengthening of the US dollar, and adverse spillovers from global supply chain disruptions posed upside risks to the inflation outlook,” it said. These risks were, however, expected to be largely offset by downside risks emanating from fiscal consolidation, improved food supply conditions, and exchange rate stability. Headline inflation rose to 5.2% in September 2026, up from 5.0% in August 2026. Consumer Price Inflation went up 1.1% month-on-month in September, reversing the previous month’s trend. Food Inflation picked up to 4.0% in September from 3.0% in August, whilst non-food inflation eased slightly to 6.2% in September 2026 from 6.8% in August 2026.

items.title: APC group rallies Southeast support for Tinubu
items.description: By Vincent Ujumadu The Tinubu Support Group (TSG) in the Southeast, led by former All Progressives Congress (APC) National Auditor, Sir Paul Chukwuma, on Thursday held a rally in Awka, Anambra State, to mobilise support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027. At the rally, the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, urged voters in the zone to support APC candidates across all levels in the 2027 general elections. Chukwuma, a former governorship candidate in Anambra State, and the APC senatorial candidate for Anambra Central, Uche Ekwunife, also urged voters to support Tinubu and other candidates of the party. They expressed confidence that the APC would secure substantial votes across the five Southeast states, arguing that Tinubu’s actions and policies had earned him support in the region. However, some APC leaders in Anambra State reportedly expressed dissatisfaction with what they described as the party’s national leadership relying on the strength of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) to secure votes for Tinubu in the state. The APC state secretary, Sir Obiora Okpala, said the party should be adequately recognised in political arrangements in Anambra, given its status as the ruling party at the national level and a major political stakeholder in the state. He argued that the APC should be carried along in the process, rather than APGA being given what he described as undue advantage over the party in Anambra. items.title: Chinese FM meets Russian counterpart in Azerbaijan
items.description: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Wednesday met with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, in Baku, with both sides pledging to strengthen bilateral cooperation and coordination in multilateral frameworks. Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, congratulated Russia on the successful State Duma elections. Wang expressed confidence that the upcoming APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen in November would achieve fruitful results with support from Russia and other parties, injecting strong momentum into development and cooperation in the Asia-Pacific. He also called for closer cooperation among members of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) to uphold genuine multilateralism and contribute to improving global governance. Lavrov said Russia-China relations and cooperation across various fields had continued to advance under the strategic guidance of the two countries' leaders, serving their fundamental interests. He reaffirmed Russia's full support for China's hosting of the APEC meeting and called for closer coordination within the United Nations, the Group of 20, APEC and BRICS to safeguard international fairness and justice. The two sides also coordinated positions on upcoming high-level exchanges and international and regional issues of mutual concern, reaching new common understandings.

15 octobre 1987 : 39 ans après, Thomas Sankara continue de vivre à travers ses idéaux et les générations
items.description: 39 années se sont écoulées depuis l'assassinat du capitaine Thomas Sankara et de ses douze compagnons, le 15 octobre 1987. Mais le temps n'a visiblement pas effacé le souvenir du père de la Révolution burkinabè. Ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026, le Mémorial Thomas Sankara, à Ouagadougou, a accueilli la cérémonie nationale d'hommage aux victimes de cette tragédie. Présidée par le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, représentant le président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, cette commémoration a été marquée par un appel à l'unité, à la souveraineté et à la poursuite du combat révolutionnaire. Entre émotion, souvenirs et espoir, les participants ont témoigné de la place qu'occupe toujours Thomas Sankara dans la conscience collective. Au Mémorial qui porte désormais son nom, à Ouagadougou, la commémoration de ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026 a été l'occasion de se souvenir de l'homme, mais aussi de questionner l'héritage qu'il a laissé à la nation burkinabè et au-delà de ses frontières. Dans le discours du président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, prononcé par le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, une conviction a été réaffirmée : l'assassinat de Thomas Sankara n'a pas entraîné la disparition de ses idéaux. « Une idée ne meurt pas sous les balles assassines de l'adversité ; elle meurt seulement lorsqu'on cesse de la défendre », a déclaré le chef de l'État dans son message. Revenant sur les quatre années de la Révolution démocratique et populaire, de 1983 à 1987, il a rappelé les transformations engagées dans un pays alors confronté à d'importants défis de développement. Des millions d'arbres plantés, des villages dotés de dispensaires et d'écoles, la promotion des femmes aux hautes sphères de décision, la construction d'infrastructures et la reconquête de la dignité nationale figurent parmi les acquis évoqués. Pour le président du Faso, ces réalisations constituent la démonstration qu'un peuple peut, par sa volonté et son travail, prendre son destin en main. Tirer les leçons du 15 octobre pour préserver l'unité Au-delà de l'hommage, le discours présidentiel a accordé une place importante aux enseignements politiques de l'assassinat de Thomas Sankara. Le chef de l'État a notamment rappelé que le père de la Révolution était tombé sous les coups de ceux qui partageaient sa table, son uniforme et son serment. Une tragédie dont il invite les Burkinabè à retenir les conséquences des divisions internes. « La leçon du 15 octobre est éloquente : une révolution ne meurt pas seulement de la méchanceté de ses ennemis du dehors ; elle meurt, avant tout, de la division fratricide de ses propres gardiens », a-t-il souligné. Dans cette dynamique, il a appelé à combattre la calomnie, la méfiance et les ambitions personnelles susceptibles de fragiliser la cohésion nationale. « Il est temps que ceux qui travaillent à nous diviser comprennent que le Burkina Faso de 2026 n'est pas celui de 1987 », a-t-il averti, faisant notamment référence à la mobilisation populaire du 30 septembre dernier, à l'occasion du quatrième anniversaire de la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP). Pour le président Ibrahim Traoré, le plus bel hommage à Thomas Sankara et aux autres victimes des événements du 15 octobre 1987 et des jours suivants ne réside pas uniquement dans les cérémonies commémoratives. Il se traduit également par l'engagement quotidien des Burkinabè, chacun dans son domaine d'activité. Le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a livré le message du président du Faso, le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré À lire : 38ᵉ année de l'assassinat de Thomas Sankara : Désormais un cérémonial militaire tous les premiers jeudis du mois en l'honneur du père de la Révolution Il a ainsi salué les Forces de défense et de sécurité, les Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie, les paysans, les travailleurs, les artistes, les artisans, les jeunes et les femmes qui contribuent, à leur manière, à la construction nationale. Réaffirmant la pertinence de la pensée économique sankariste, le chef de l'État a rappelé la nécessité de « consommer ce que nous produisons et produire ce que nous consommons ». « L'émancipation ne se décrète pas dans les discours ; elle se construit dans les champs, dans les usines, dans les laboratoires », a-t-il insisté. Entre émotion et espoir, un héritage qui continue de rassembler Parmi les participants à cette commémoration, l'émotion reste perceptible, même après près de quatre décennies. Pour Martin Zongo, administrateur général du Carrefour international du théâtre de Ouagadougou (CITO), chaque visite au Mémorial ravive le souvenir douloureux de cette journée. « Quand on vient au Mémorial, on a le cœur serré parce que nous rendons hommage certes à notre héros, mais il nous manque beaucoup. Il y a 39 ans que la tragédie s'est produite, et chaque fois qu'on s'en rappelle, on a l'impression que c'était hier », confie-t-il. Mais à la tristesse se mêle désormais une forme de satisfaction : celle de voir Thomas Sankara retrouver toute sa place dans la mémoire nationale. « Nous essuyons nos larmes, car c'est ce que lui-même nous a enseigné. Quand on admire quelqu'un, on ne le pleure pas. Ça nous remplit de joie de savoir que notre héros est immortalisé et que personne ne va l'oublier », poursuit Martin Zongo. Il estime qu'après plusieurs décennies durant lesquelles la mémoire de Thomas Sankara a été reléguée au second plan, l'intérêt renouvelé pour son œuvre constitue une évolution importante qu'il souhaite voir se poursuivre. Les officiels ont visité le Panthéon des figures panafricanistes et révolutionnaires du Mémorial Pour Adeline Tougma, juriste et artisane, admiratrice de Thomas Sankara, le 15 octobre 1987 a laissé un vide profond dans la trajectoire du pays. Elle considère néanmoins que la génération actuelle, malgré un contexte marqué par l'insécurité et le terrorisme, porte la responsabilité de poursuivre le travail engagé. À ses yeux, aucun projet national durable ne peut se construire dans la dispersion des énergies. « Si vous luttez seul et que je lutte seule, on va s'en sortir doucement chacun dans son coin. Mais si on se sacrifie, nous aurons un futur de bien-être pour nos enfants, pour les générations à venir… », explique-t-elle, invitant les Burkinabè à privilégier l'intérêt collectif. Elle voit dans la dynamique engagée par le capitaine Ibrahim Traoré une continuité du combat révolutionnaire et appelle à l'accompagner. La présence du Mémorial lui rappelle également la pensée de Kwame Nkrumah, notamment son attachement à l'unité africaine. Une aspiration qu'elle estime indissociable des idéaux défendus par Thomas Sankara. De son côté, Me Bénéwendé Stanislas Sankara considère que la renaissance de la pensée sankariste dépasse aujourd'hui le cadre des commémorations. « On vit ce dynamisme de la renaissance du père de la Révolution, le capitaine Thomas Sankara, en chaque Burkinabè », affirme-t-il. Il relève particulièrement l'engagement de la jeunesse depuis l'avènement de la Révolution progressiste populaire, tout en soulignant que les idéaux de Thomas Sankara continuent de mobiliser bien au-delà du Burkina Faso, notamment dans l'espace de l'Alliance des États du Sahel (AES). Pour lui, trente-neuf ans après l'assassinat du capitaine, les fondations posées par la Révolution demeurent des repères pour les générations à venir. Me Bénéwendé Stanislas Sankara, Martin Zongo et Adeline Tougma saluent la renaissance des idéaux de Thomas Sankara et appellent à poursuivre son combat dans l'unité, pour les générations présentes et futures. Plus de 200 000 visiteurs au Mémorial Thomas Sankara L'intérêt que suscite toujours le père de la Révolution se mesure également à la fréquentation du Mémorial qui lui est consacré. Selon les chiffres communiqués dans le discours présidentiel, depuis l'ouverture des visites au public, le 19 mai 2025, jusqu'au 30 septembre 2026, le site a enregistré plus de 200 000 visiteurs, générant environ 130 millions de francs CFA au profit du Projet de construction des infrastructures du Mémorial Thomas Sankara (PCIM-INTS). Le président du Faso a salué les contributions des institutions, des organisations et des particuliers à travers la campagne « Ma brique pour Sankara ». Il a invité les Burkinabè ainsi que les sympathisants du père de la Révolution d'août 1983 à poursuivre leur mobilisation pour l'édification du site. L'ambition affichée est de faire du Mémorial bien davantage qu'un lieu de recueillement. « Que le Mémorial devienne aussi une bibliothèque à ciel ouvert de la mémoire, un espace de débat pour la jeunesse, un lieu où l'on vient apprendre à servir », a souhaité le chef de l'État. Il a également salué l'initiative de la municipalité du troisième arrondissement de Rome, en Italie, qui a récemment baptisé un parc du nom de Thomas Sankara. Un geste qu'il considère comme une reconnaissance de la portée internationale de son héritage. Le vice-président du Comité international du mémorial Thomas Sankara, Blaise Sanon À lire : Mémorial Thomas-Sankara : Au-delà du souvenir, un héritage à transmettre Enfin, une pensée particulière a été adressée aux autres victimes des événements qui ont suivi le 15 octobre 1987, notamment à Ouagadougou, Koudougou et Pô, ainsi qu'à leurs familles. Farida Thiombiano Lefaso.net

items.title: Cannabis légal : 1.100 hectares récoltés et près de 1.500 autorisations retirées pour non-respect des procédures
items.description: La campagne de récolte du cannabis au titre de la saison agricole 2026 progresse au Maroc. Dans la province de Taounate, la récolte de la variété locale, dite « beldia », est achevée à 92 %. À l’échelle des trois provinces où la culture est autorisée, 1.100 hectares ont été récoltés, soit 60 % de la superficie totale consacrée à cette variété, selon les données relatives à l’évolution de la filière légale du cannabis. Dans le même temps, l’Agence nationale de réglementation des activités relatives au cannabis (ANRAC) intensifie ses contrôles. Au total, 1.490 autorisations ont été retirées pour non-respect des procédures réglementaires. Cette mesure concerne aussi bien les activités agricoles que les différents maillons de la chaîne de production, de transformation et de commercialisation du cannabis. Les superficies concernées mobilisent quelque 1.800 agriculteurs regroupés au sein de 154 coopératives, dans le cadre du dispositif légal mis en place par le Maroc pour encadrer cette filière. La culture et les activités commerciales sous surveillance Taounate figure parmi les provinces les plus avancées dans les opérations de récolte, avec un taux d’achèvement de 92 % pour la variété locale. Le calendrier est différent pour la variété importée, dont la récolte a débuté en octobre et devrait se poursuivre jusqu’en décembre 2026. Ce décalage s’explique par les différences entre les cycles de maturation des deux variétés. Au-delà du suivi de la campagne agricole, l’ANRAC entend faire respecter les règles encadrant l’exploitation légale du cannabis. Sur les 1.490 autorisations retirées, près de 1.300 concernaient des agriculteurs exerçant une activité de culture. Les 190 autres avaient été délivrées à des opérateurs intervenant dans les autres segments de la filière. Le détail des retraits fait état de 60 autorisations d’importation de semences, de 45 autorisations de transformation et de fabrication, de 35 autorisations de commercialisation, de 31 autorisations d’exportation, de 12 autorisations d’exportation de semences et de sept autorisations de transport. Ces chiffres illustrent l’étendue du dispositif de contrôle, qui couvre l’ensemble de la chaîne, depuis la production agricole jusqu’aux activités industrielles, commerciales et logistiques. L’objectif est de conditionner l’exercice de ces activités au respect des exigences légales et réglementaires applicables à chaque étape, de la production à la valorisation des produits. Le label marocain à la conquête des marchés européens Parallèlement à ce renforcement des contrôles, l’ANRAC cherche à consolider la présence des produits marocains à base de cannabis sur les marchés internationaux. L’Agence a engagé des démarches visant à protéger, à l’échelle internationale, le logo propre à ces produits. Elle a déjà reçu des notifications confirmant la protection de ce signe distinctif au Luxembourg et au Portugal. Des notifications similaires sont attendues dans les prochains mois dans d’autres pays européens, notamment en Allemagne et en Espagne. Le logo « Produit du cannabis » a vocation à garantir l’authenticité des produits marocains qui en sont porteurs et à renforcer la crédibilité de la filière nationale auprès des partenaires étrangers. Il doit permettre de mieux identifier les produits concernés et de les distinguer sur les marchés extérieurs. Selon les données communiquées, cette protection vise également à soutenir le positionnement des opérateurs marocains sous le label « Made in Morocco », dans le respect des normes internationales, et à améliorer les perspectives de développement des produits nationaux à l’étranger. Au-delà de la réglementation de la culture, le Maroc cherche ainsi à structurer une filière intégrée, capable de générer davantage de valeur ajoutée grâce à la transformation, à la fabrication, à la commercialisation et à l’exportation. La protection de l’identité des produits et la garantie de leur origine constituent, dans cette perspective, des leviers pour renforcer la confiance des partenaires internationaux. items.title: Sammi Awuku urges NPP Germany to unite ahead of 2028 elections
items.description: New Patriotic Party (NPP) Member of Parliament for Akuapem North, Sammi Awuku, has urged the party’s Germany Branch to prioritise unity, humility and collective commitment as it prepares for the 2028 general elections. He said the newly elected national executives and party structures at all levels must work together to strengthen the NPP and position it to regain power in 2028. Mr Awuku made the call when he addressed members of the NPP Germany Branch during a Thanksgiving Service and Unity Dinner held in Hannover from October 9 to 10, 2026. The two-day event began with an Islamic prayer session in Frankfurt on Friday and ended with a Christian worship service and Unity Dinner at Hütten Str. 228 in Hannover on Saturday. The gathering was attended by NPP MP for New Juaben South Michael O. Baafi, Member of the NPP National Council of Elders Eileen Mary Posch-Oduro, Mayor of Mündenheim Rheinland-Pfalz Raymond Höptner, NPP Germany Branch Chairman Dr Nana B. Enninful and Hannover Chapter Chairman Bright Otchere. Mr Awuku described his visit as that of a “John the Baptist”, saying it was intended to prepare the ground for an anticipated engagement between the NPP Germany Branch and former Vice-President Dr Mahamudu Bawumia on November 21. Dr Bawumia is expected to visit Germany at the invitation of the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung and interact with members of the NPP Germany Branch. Mr Awuku said the new national executives needed the cooperation of all party members and structures to enable the NPP to effectively campaign for the 2028 presidential election. He also stressed the importance of the party’s external branches in contributing to efforts to address what he described as Ghana’s current socio-economic challenges. Leadership Mr Awuku reminded party members that the NPP belonged to everyone who served it and urged them to support the newly elected executives. He called on the leadership of the Germany Branch, particularly its chairman, Dr Nana Benyin Enninful, to exercise humility, respect and selflessness in the discharge of their responsibilities. “A mandate is a privilege, not a licence to disregard others; trust must be earned through service,” he said. “A leader who wins the hearts of the people strengthens the office; one who loses their trust weakens it.” Drawing on his experience as a young party organiser, Mr Awuku said his success in previous youth and national organiser contests demonstrated the importance of mobilising and working with party members. He used the proverb, “It is the feathers that make the bird beautiful,” to emphasise the contribution of individual members to the strength and influence of the party. Criticism of government Turning to national politics, Mr Awuku described the work of the NPP’s 87 opposition MPs as challenging but said they would remain committed to what they considered to be Ghana’s best interests. He criticised the government’s performance in areas including education, health, sports and industry. He also raised concerns about the implementation of the government’s 24-hour economy policy and cited what he described as a failure to secure placement for more than 50,000 Junior High School graduates. He urged Ghanaians in the country and abroad to remain actively engaged in the political process. He also encouraged members of the diaspora to engage their families in Ghana on the NPP’s policies and vision ahead of the 2028 elections. Mr Awuku urged the Germany Branch to put past challenges behind it and concentrate on rebuilding its structures and strengthening its mobilisation efforts. “Unity is not a slogan; it is the work members do together,” he said. “When leaders serve with humility and members contribute with commitment, the whole Branch becomes stronger.” Other speakers at the event also appealed to members to support the NPP and contribute to efforts to strengthen the party ahead of the 2028 general elections.

Dans un communiqué publié jeudi, le ministère a indiqué que les listes des étudiants concernés avaient été transmises à la délégation « Taazour » et à la société de transports publics, invitant les bénéficiaires à effectuer les démarches nécessaires pour obtenir leur abonnement. Le ministère a précisé que l’achat des billets à tarif réduit, dont le prix unitaire est de 50 anciennes ouguiyas, est désormais disponible exclusivement via l’application, soulignant que les étudiants qui ne l’utilisent pas devront payer le prix normal du billet. Le ministère a également annoncé la mise en service de bus du système de transport rapide « BHNS » sur des lignes urbaines desservant le campus universitaire, en réponse aux demandes des usagers.

items.title: How Pete Hegseth’s Plan for a Reality-TV Execution Imploded
items.description: D efense Secretary Pete Hegseth has enjoyed President Trump’s full support for any number of Trumpian initiatives: staging macho, campy shows of military bravado; trashing political opponents and the press, often by name; dissing European allies; posting videos of air strikes on suspected drug boats off the coast of Latin America. But Hegseth apparently crossed a line with his revelation last week that the execution by firing squad of a military death-row inmate would be livestreamed to the world. Even a president who’d brought a bloody mixed-martial-arts fight to the White House lawn apparently didn’t relish the thought of an afternoon spent watching Army soldiers shoot bullets into a paraplegic. From the start, Hegseth’s plan for the death of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people in a 2009 rampage at Fort Hood, in Texas, was haphazard. Trump approved the death sentence on October 2. Then the Army announced on October 6 that Hasan, who has been on death row since 2013, would be killed in December by firing squad rather than by lethal injection, the method used in many civilian executions. Two days later, Hegseth told the podcaster Jack Posobiec (known for his promotion of the Pizzagate pedophile conspiracy theory) that Hasan’s execution would be public. Hegseth confirmed later that day on X that the execution would not be “public” in the typical style of a state-governed execution—conducted in the presence of officials, victims’ relatives, and maybe a few journalists—but rather broadcast via livestream. Trump was immediately inundated with feedback from friends and confidants, including a number of lawmakers who told the president that Hegseth’s plan was a terrible idea, one close Trump adviser told us. On October 9, Trump appeared to signal his approval for Hegseth’s idea. But in remarks in subsequent days, Trump equivocated. “I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision,” he said. Within the administration, there was immediate and “pretty universal revulsion” about the livestream plan, one administration official told us. By late last week, even the president’s inner circle was making its distaste clear. Vice President Vance barely hid his disgust. “If it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not gonna be watching it,” he told reporters. One administration official told us that Vance’s response reflected his general frustration with Hegseth, who, like Vance, is said to harbor 2028 presidential ambitions. Then House Speaker Mike Johnson followed suit: He, too, would sit out the Hasan-execution show. Other lawmakers kept calling the president and his aides to say that a livestream not only was barbaric but could also undermine Republican efforts to hold on to Congress in the midterm elections . Between those private calls and criticism on TV over the weekend that Trump watched, the president “soured on it pretty quickly,” one adviser told us. Hegseth’s livestream plan was a surprise to virtually everyone at the Pentagon; even those in Hegseth’s closest circle of advisers were blindsided, people familiar with the matter told us. Few in the military objected to the idea of Hasan’s execution, given that he’d committed the despicable act of service-member fratricide. Still, the optics of shooting a person who is paralyzed from the waist down—Hasan was shot while being apprehended by authorities on the day of his rampage—made even battle-hardened warriors uneasy. “One of the more immediate reactions was: Does Hegseth realize this guy is in a wheelchair? ” one official told us. Across the military and intelligence communities, officials also worried that a public execution of a Muslim would become a recruiting tool for groups such as the Islamic State. Hasan was apparently motivated to kill by his objection to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. “A lot of people think it’ll be turned into propaganda for an organization that’s been dying a slow death for the last decade,” the official said of ISIS, which has repeatedly used videotaped executions of hostages as a recruitment tool. Representative Austin Scott, a Georgia Republican and a member of the House Armed Services Committee, wrote on X that although he supported Hasan’s death sentence, “live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that.” Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called Hegseth’s plan “beyond disgusting.” Today, Trump said on Truth Social that livestreaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists,” but “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die.” The White House had no further comment. The whole affair may provide new grist for the growing number of Republicans who are unhappy with Hegseth’s performance, especially as the Iran war has become bogged down. Trump has remained a resolute supporter of the Pentagon chief, officials have told us. But plenty in Trump’s own party would now not be unhappy to see the president’s attitude change. Hegseth, for his part, quickly walked away from his own proposed reality-TV spectacle. Trump and Hegseth spoke about today’s reversal ahead of the president’s social-media announcement, according to Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson. “They are completely aligned,” Parnell told us in a statement. [ Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] Hasan will still be executed, as planned, by firing squad at Fort Hood on December 3 at 1 p.m. central standard time, but only a select audience will witness the event. The Pentagon hopes that his killing will be more efficient than the last time a service member faced an official firing squad. On January 31, 1945, near Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, France, the Army executed Private Eddie Slovik, 24 years old, over his desertion during World War II. Slovik had admitted to the crime, and a court martial convicted him in November 1944. His appeal for clemency was denied by General Dwight D. Eisenhower. The execution was intended, in part, to deter other troops from leaving their post amid heavy battlefield casualties in the final year of the war. Slovik was strapped to a wooden post, stripped of his military insignia, and blindfolded. The firing squad struck him 11 times. But the bullets missed his heart, leaving Slovik to bleed to death. Nancy A. Youssef contributed reporting.

items.title: Le Sénégal prévoit un déficit budgétaire d’environ un trillion de francs CFA pour 2027
items.description: Le gouvernement sénégalais a annoncé que le projet de budget 2027 prévoit des dépenses s'élevant à 7 363,7 milliards de francs CFA (environ 13 milliards de dollars), pour des recettes estimées à 6 012,1 milliards de francs, un déficit de 1 351,7 milliards de francs, soit 4,7 % du produit intérieur brut. Le gouvernement vise à porter les recettes fiscales à 5 044,6 milliards de francs, dans le cadre de ses efforts pour renforcer les ressources de l’État et réduire le déficit budgétaire. Le projet de budget, présenté au Parlement, prévoit une augmentation des dotations allouées au programme de transferts monétaires en faveur des familles bénéficiaires des « aides à la sécurité familiale » à 140 milliards de francs, contre 70 milliards auparavant. Le gouvernement prévoit également d’orienter les dépenses vers le soutien à la production locale, à l’emploi et à l’investissement, dans le cadre du programme de transformation nationale « Sénégal 2050 », tout en s’efforçant de maîtriser les dépenses et d’améliorer le recouvrement des impôts.

items.title: CSACEFA seeks end to child marriage, demands more investment in girls’ education
items.description: By Chioma Obinna The Coalition of Civil Society Action for Education for All (CSACEFA), Lagos State Chapter, has called for increased investment in girls’ education, stronger child protection measures and coordinated efforts to end child marriage and ensure that girls have access to quality education. The coalition made the call at its Lagos Education Summit and International Day of the Girl Child 2026, held at the State Universal Basic Education Board (SUBEB) Hall, Maryland, Lagos, with the theme, “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights.” Speaking at the event, CSACEFA Lagos Coordinator, Stella Olubunmi Francis, said every child deserved access to quality education, irrespective of gender or personal circumstances. Francis expressed concern over the stigma and discrimination faced by pregnant schoolgirls, urging stakeholders to create opportunities for them to continue their education. “There is a lot of stigma and shame, but these children should not be denied education because of their pregnancies. We need to create more opportunities for them to continue their education,” she said. Representing the Executive Chairman of SUBEB, Dr Akeem Babatunde Shittu, the Board Secretary, Lamidi Akeem, reaffirmed the Lagos State Government’s commitment to children’s rights and basic education. “The Lagos State Government has already domesticated the Child Rights Act. Every government agency saddled with responsibilities concerning children, particularly SUBEB, has a role to play,” Akeem said. He acknowledged the contribution of civil society organisations and development partners to efforts aimed at bringing out-of-school children back into the education system. In her keynote address, a lawyer and member of the International Federation of Women Lawyers (FIDA) Nigeria, Mrs Olubola Afolabi, called for stronger child protection mechanisms, legal accountability and improved access to education to tackle child marriage. “Why does child marriage happen? What happens to the girls? These are the questions I want us to ask ourselves,” Afolabi said, urging stakeholders to confront the factors responsible for the practice and its consequences for girls. CSACEFA Lagos Provost and Founder of LEADIN AFRICA, Margaret ChiChi Nkire, said the summit was organised to strengthen gender-responsive education financing and inclusive budgeting in Lagos State and Nigeria. During a panel session she moderated, participants called for rights-based education policies, the removal of hidden charges that undermine free education and improved support for pregnant, married and parenting girls to remain in school or return without discrimination. “We hope that beyond this summit, we will have better coordination among stakeholders. We have Plan International, Save the Children, the British Council, SUBEB, the National Human Rights Commission and other stakeholders here today,” Nkire said. Representing Plan International Nigeria, Aishatu Usman Bukar stressed the need for adequate and sustainable education funding, gender-responsive budgeting and measures to remove financial barriers facing girls and vulnerable households. A student participant, Esther Matthew, said the summit had broadened her understanding of the opportunities available to girls beyond marriage. “I have learnt that being a girl child is not only about marriage. A girl can stand on her own, become a business owner and achieve whatever she wants in the future,” Matthew said. She also pledged to act on the message, “See Something, Say Something,” by intervening where possible when she encountered situations threatening children’s safety and reporting cases beyond her capacity to a teacher or another trusted adult. The summit featured discussions on child marriage, inclusive education and sustainable financing, alongside cultural dance and spoken-word performances celebrating the girl child. Other participants included representatives of Save the Children International Nigeria, the National Association of Proprietors of Private Schools, Child Protection Network Lagos, the National Youth Council of Nigeria, mothers’ associations and School-Based Management Committees. The stakeholders called for stronger collaboration among government agencies, civil society organisations, development partners, schools and communities to protect girls’ rights and ensure that poverty, pregnancy, early marriage and discrimination do not deprive them of education. The post CSACEFA seeks end to child marriage, demands more investment in girls’ education appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Cimetière Al Ihsane : 118 hectares pour désengorger les cimetières de Casablanca
items.description: Dimensionné pour les besoins des quarante prochaines années, le projet a fait l’objet d’une visite de terrain des principaux responsables de la région. Dans le cadre du suivi des projets structurants et du renforcement des équipements de proximité, le président du Conseil de la région Casablanca-Settat, Abdellatif Maâzouz, le wali de la région, Mohamed Mhidia, et le gouverneur de la province de Médiouna, Ali Salem Chagaf, se sont rendus ce jeudi 15 octobre 2026 au cimetière Al Ihsane, dans la commune de Sidi Hajjaj Oued Hassar. La visite a permis de découvrir les aménagements réalisés sur le site et les différentes composantes de ce projet à vocation sociale, présenté comme une réponse concrète aux besoins croissants des habitants de Casablanca et de sa périphérie. Une réponse à la pression sur les cimetières existants Les cimetières actuels de Casablanca connaissent une pression croissante. Le cimetière Al Ihsane doit contribuer à la réduire à long terme, en offrant un espace aménagé conforme aux exigences de l’inhumation, dans le respect des défunts et de la dignité de leurs familles, indique un communiqué de la région Casablanca-Settat. 118 hectares et un programme complet Le projet s’étend sur environ 118 hectares et a été conçu pour couvrir les besoins prévisibles des quarante prochaines années. Il comprend les espaces d’inhumation, des locaux administratifs, des logements de fonction, des sanitaires et un parking, ainsi que des espaces verts, une mosquée et une école coranique. Le coût global s’élève à 75 millions de dirhams. La région Casablanca-Settat y a contribué à hauteur de 30 millions, ce qui, selon le communiqué, confirme son rôle dans la réalisation d’initiatives à impact social et territorial, en coordination avec les autorités locales et les partenaires concernés. Le terrain est un don d’un bienfaiteur aujourd’hui décédé, un geste humanitaire empreint de solidarité et d’entraide, souligne le communiqué. The post Cimetière Al Ihsane : 118 hectares pour désengorger les cimetières de Casablanca appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: The Inconvenient Truth: We cannot pray for the cure while protecting the disease
items.description: Africa’s greatest obstacle is not that we fail to see what ails us, but that we have grown comfortable defending it. The unborn child will inherit our choices, not our excuses. By Ing. Prof. Douglas Boateng, Chartered Director UK | Chartered Engineer UK | Fellow, Institute of Directors UK | Fellow, Ghana Institution of Engineering | Governance, Industrialisation and Supply Chain Strategist | Founder, Boardroom Governance Summit | Founder and Scriber, NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) A doctor will tell you that the most difficult patient to treat is not the one who is unaware of his illness. It is the one who knows exactly what is wrong, understands the consequences, has access to treatment, and still defends the habits that are making him sick. Yet when whole societies behave in the same way, we tend to give it gentler names: politics, culture, loyalty, survival, or simply the way things are done. This is one of the most uncomfortable truths facing many developing societies, including our own. Our greatest difficulty is not that we fail to see what ails us. It is that we see it clearly, sometimes defend its causes, and still expect our children to inherit a healthy nation. We complain about corruption while admiring unexplained wealth that happens to benefit us. We condemn indiscipline while seeking exemptions from the rules that inconvenience us. We denounce environmental destruction while buying from, financing or shielding those responsible. Then we raise our hands and pray for national transformation. Even the most generous rain, however, cannot yield a healthy harvest from soil the farmer insists on poisoning. NyansaKasa: “A society that protects the causes of its suffering should not expect time alone to deliver the cure.” When The Abnormal Becomes Normal Corruption, inequality and weak institutions are not uniquely African conditions. The real danger begins when abnormal behaviour becomes normal and normal behaviour starts to look strange. Consider the procurement officer who insists on due process and is accused of delaying progress. Consider the board director who raises an uncomfortable question about a doubtful investment, only to be met with the kind of glances usually reserved for someone who has arrived at a funeral carrying a trumpet. And consider the citizen who refuses a dishonest arrangement and is gently advised to “be realistic”. Since when did being realistic mean making peace with what is wrong? What once shocked us becomes familiar; what is familiar becomes tolerated; what is tolerated becomes defended; and what is defended eventually becomes institutionalised. At that point a society is no longer merely suffering from a problem. It is helping the problem survive. NyansaKasa(words of wisdom): “When wrongdoing becomes ordinary and integrity becomes exceptional, society has not merely lost its standards; it has reversed its moral compass.” When Political Colours Decide Right And Wrong Political competition is healthy and necessary. It becomes unhealthy, however, when party loyalty replaces moral consistency. Too often, a questionable contract is condemned when linked to opponents and explained away when linked to allies. The evidence stays the same; only the colours change. It is almost as though morality alters its chemical composition whenever a government changes, becoming poisonous in opposition and medicinal in power. This observation is not aimed at any party, government or country; it describes a human weakness that crosses borders. Its cost, however, is real. When wrongdoing is judged by affiliation, institutions lose authority, citizens lose confidence, and accountability becomes selective. A nation must always be larger than the parties competing to govern it. The Environment Does Not Accept Our Excuses Nowhere is the contradiction more visible than in how we treat our land and water. In January 2025, Ghana Water shut its Bonsa headworks, which supplied about 75 per cent of the drinking water for Tarkwa Nsuaem, because illegal mining had so polluted the river that, in the plant manager’s words, it had become “just mud”. Such activity is sustained by a web of financiers, operators, buyers, weak enforcement, economic hardship and social tolerance. At times the same community that demands government action also expects enforcement officers to spare particular relatives, friends or the politically connected. That is rather like a patient demanding treatment while threatening the doctor who tries to remove the infection. Flooding tells a similar story. On 3 June 2015, floodwaters and a fire at a fuel station near Kwame Nkrumah Circle in Accra claimed more than 150 lives. A decade later, drains remain choked with refuse and structures still sit across waterways, yet whenever the streets flood, rainfall becomes the principal suspect. Polluted water, after all, does not ask for party membership before it enters a household. NyansaKasa(words of wisdom): “A nation cannot continuously block its waterways with yesterday’s indiscipline and expect tomorrow’s rainfall to negotiate politely.” Corruption Is Never A Solo Performance Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index scored Ghana 43 out of 100, against a sub Saharan average of 32, while UNCTAD estimates that Africa loses about $88.6 billion every year to illicit financial flows, more than the continent receives in development aid. It is convenient, but incomplete, to treat corruption as something that begins and ends with public officials. Corruption usually depends on a chain of participants: someone offers, someone receives, someone prepares the documents, someone approves, someone conceals, and many remain silent in the hope of eventually benefiting. When communities celebrate wealth without asking where it came from, when families press relatives in office for favours beyond legitimate means, and when businesses treat bribery as an ordinary operating cost, we collectively create the rewards that make misconduct attractive. Change is possible. Singapore, through decades of sustained enforcement, now scores 84 and ranks third in the world, and closer to home Seychelles (68), Cape Verde (62), Botswana and Rwanda (58 each) show that African nations can rise well above the regional average. Africa need not copy any model mechanically, but the lesson is clear: consistent rules and credible consequences matter. NyansaKasa(words of wisdom): “When society applauds unexplained wealth more loudly than honest achievement, it should not be surprised when integrity struggles to attract investors.” Governance Begins At Home We often speak of governance as though it starts in Parliament, the boardroom or the courts. Much of it starts at the family table. Children learn early whether promises are kept, whether rules apply equally and whether dishonesty is excused. A parent who condemns corruption on television but celebrates a favour secured through connections is teaching two lessons at once, and the child may remember the practical one more vividly. Government carries heavy responsibilities that cannot be delegated, from competent leadership to security, justice and a productive economy. Citizens, equally, carry duties no government can perform on their behalf, from paying legitimate taxes and disposing of waste responsibly to rejecting bribery and demanding evidence. Blaming government for everything is as incomplete as blaming citizens for systemic failure. NyansaKasa(words of wisdom): “Government may steer the national vehicle, but citizens who continuously remove its wheels should not complain that the journey is slow.” We must also resist confusing activity with progress. A bridge that is 95 percent complete is of little comfort to the stranded traveller; development must be judged by outcomes, not announcements. The Path To Recovery Reversing the trend begins with honest diagnosis, separating symptoms from causes and resisting explanations chosen for political comfort. It requires enforcement that is consistent, lawful and fair, because laws applied selectively lose their moral force. It demands institutional continuity, so that useful policies survive changes of government, as South Korea demonstrates: around 1960 its income per person was broadly similar to Ghana’s, yet decades of patient institution building have since made it many times richer. It calls for incentives that protect whistleblowers and reward competence, and for boards that insist on effective audit and ethics oversight. And it needs schools, traditional authorities, faith communities and professional bodies that cultivate civic responsibility and own the change. Above all, it requires each of us to stop treating personal responsibility as something meant mainly for other people. This is not an invitation to blame ourselves, but to examine ourselves, which is where lasting change begins. The Unborn Child Will Inherit Our Choices The consequences of what we tolerate rarely end with our generation. A polluted river does not run clean because the official who ignored it has retired. Imagine an African child born 25 years from now who studies the records and discovers that we knew. Experts warned, committees investigated and governments promised, yet too many of us kept protecting the behaviours behind the problems. What would we tell that child? That the offenders belonged to our party? That everyone else was doing the same? NyansaKasa(words of wisdom): “The unborn child cannot vote against today’s mistakes, yet tomorrow that child may spend a lifetime paying for decisions made before birth.” A sick society can recover. But no doctor can permanently cure a patient determined to protect the disease. Perhaps, then, our national question should no longer be simply “What is wrong with our country?” but the more courageous one: “Which of the things we know are wrong do we continue to tolerate, excuse, celebrate or personally benefit from?” The honest answer may implicate institutions we belong to, parties we support, customs we inherited and, at times, the person in the mirror. Africa’s future does not require a continent without problems. It requires a continent increasingly unwilling to defend their causes. Let us stop protecting the disease while praying for the cure, and stop confusing loyalty with complicity. The unborn African child will not inherit our intentions, only the consequences of our choices. The Africa we desire is in our own hands, and so too is the Africa we may one day regret leaving behind. About the Author Ing. Professor Douglas K. Boateng is a strategist in governance, industrialisation and supply chains, and serves as a professional chairperson, an international Chartered Director (UK) and a Chartered Engineer (UK). A Pan-Africanist and social entrepreneur at heart, he has spent his career working across public institutions, corporate boards and industrial policy, in Africa and beyond, guided by the conviction that strong institutions are built one honest decision at a time. His contributions to industry and academia have earned him more than six lifetime achievement awards. He is the founder of NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom), a collection of daily aphorisms he has written and shared since late 2019, distilling decades of experience advising governments, boards, and enterprises on governance, accountability, and institutional resilience into words meant to challenge and endure. He convenes the Boardroom Governance Summit, Africa’s largest boardroom-focused summit, and writes a widely read weekly op-ed series titled “Inconvenient Truth” and “What Is Wrong With Us”, featured on some of the region’s leading digital media platforms. Professor Boateng can be reached via LinkedIn or at info@panavest.com .

items.title: UK threatens to ban Eritreans over migrant return policy
items.description: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritreans from entering the UK if the East African country’s government does not accept more returns of small boat migrants and foreign national offenders. From Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movement outside London. Fast-track visas will also be stopped for VIPs. Ministers have previously pressured other countries into accepting returns by threatening visa bans. Eritrea branded the move a “perfunctory political gimmick”, saying the UK had not issued a single visa to an Eritrean official since 2023, which the Home Office denies. The country’s embassy in London also accused the UK of refusing to engage in “meaningful and appropriate dialogue”. It said the UK had failed to disclose the return of criminals still serving prison terms and had claimed the returns were voluntary, “when clearly, they were not”. However, a Home Office spokesperson said the Eritrean government’s commentary “misrepresents the UK’s position”. The UK had granted an exemption from immigration control for an Eritrean official in August 2026, according to the Home Office. Sources also said the UK hoped to restore co-operation between the two countries. Human Rights Watch has accused Eritrea’s government of widespread repression – including forced labour, conscription and restrictions on freedom of expression. Eritreans were the most common nationality among small boat migrants in the 12 months to June – accounting for 18% of arrivals , according to figures from the House of Commons Library. Mahmood said: “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused.” She said she would not hesitate “to impose further measures on other countries refusing to co-operate”. The UK government accused the Eritrean authorities of “abruptly” withdrawing co-operation earlier this year. The restrictions mean diplomats are banned from travelling 60km outside London without permission. The Home Office said this mirrored restrictions on British officials in Eritrea’s capital Asmara. In the 12 months to June only seven people from Eritrea were returned there from the UK, according to Home Office figures. A further 244 Eritreans were returned to other countries. Over the same period, more than 5,800 Eritreans arrived in the UK via small boats. A further 1,300 were given visas, mostly to join people already settled in the UK. Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said targeting Eritrea would have little impact. “Eritrea is one of the major countries of origin for asylum seekers coming to the UK – we had roughly 7,000 asylum applications in the last year of data, roughly 8% of the total,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “Most Eritreans who come and claim asylum are not removable at all – the government would never be in negotiations to remove them because 84% are successful at initial decision; more will be successful on appeal.” She added that about 1,400 people were initially refused asylum, but that this number would reduce after appeals. Many young Eritreans try to leave the country – which is a one-party state – to avoid military conscription, which can last for decades. Eritrea has never held an election since independence from Ethiopia in 1993 and there is no independent media. Critics of President Isaias Afwerki have been arrested and jailed for many years, often without trial. Only four religions are permitted in the country – Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam, the Roman Catholic Church, and the Evangelical-Lutheran church of Eritrea – and followers of other religions have been locked up for years on end. Last November, the Home Office said it was prepared to suspend visas from countries that “fail to co-operate with the return of their citizens”. Earlier this year, the UK threatened visa restrictions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Restrictions were announced against the DRC last year, but the Home Office said these have been lifted after co-operation on returns improved. Angola and Namibia both agreed changes before restrictions were introduced. But Sumption pointed out that the government may avoid targeting certain countries to avoid damaging trade relationships. “If you’re looking at overall numbers of people who are refused asylum and not returned to their country of origin, it would be places like Pakistan, also Bangladesh that are right at the top of the list,” she said. “But the collateral damage of a ban on visas for those countries when you have so many international students coming, for example, [and] a lot of people coming on work visas would be much greater than a country like Eritrea.” According to Home Office data, more than 20,400 people have arrived in the UK by small boats so far since the beginning of this year, down 40% from the same period last year. There were more than 40,600 returns and deportations from the UK from July 2025 to June this year – an 8% increase on the same period last year. Of those who had been returned, fewer than 6,000 have been convicted of a criminal offence.
